solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Tie required in Oxford but not Wellington? (8)

definitions.text: Tie required in Oxford but not Wellington?

blocks.note: reads as a college dress code; an Oxford is also a laced leather shoe
reads as a school or a duke; a Wellington is a rubber boot pulled on with no fastening

explanation.surface: A dress code that demands a tie at Oxford University but not at Wellington College.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford and Wellington read as a university and a school, but they are footwear, so the tie is the one that fastens a shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: The only tie an Oxford shoe needs and a Wellington boot lacks is the lace that fastens it.

clue.text: Singer and old lady right at home (6)

explanation.surface: A singer who lives with their mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old lady' is slang for mother, not an elderly woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Dean Martin and Chris Martin are both famous singers.

clue.text: Ripe romp could be seen as this (8)

definitions.text: Ripe romp could be seen as this

indicators.note: the letters of the fodder can be looked at in another arrangement

explanation.surface: A bawdy frolic might strike some people as indecent.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: the letters rearrange, and a ripe romp is exactly what might be judged indecent.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripe here means risqué, and a risqué romp is the very thing prudes call indecent, so the clue reads straight.

clue.text: Charted road going north, east and west (4)

indicators.note: in a down clue, going north means reading upwards

explanation.surface: A map shows a road running in three compass directions.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass words look like the map's content, and each is just its letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To chart a coastline is to draw it on a map, so charted and drew share the mapping sense.

clue.text: Transfix reader originally entertained by article? (6)

indicators.note: the origin of a word is its first letter
a host entertains a guest inside the home

blocks.note: a piece = an article, as in a newspaper piece
first letter of Reader, placed inside PIE|CE

explanation.surface: A reader is spellbound by something in the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transfix' pretends to mean enthral, but here it means to run through; 'article' is a written piece, not a grammar word.
explanation.definitionFit: Transfix's literal sense is to run a spike right through something, which is to spear or impale it.

clue.text: English boy raised in valley (4)

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting the letters up reads them backwards

explanation.surface: An English lad who grew up in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' reads as brought up, as in childhood; here it flips ELAD upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional word: dale is the northern English name for a valley, as in the Yorkshire Dales.

clue.text: One can’t fly after Heathrow checks (4)

indicators.note: to check is to hold back, so the phrase holds the answer

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word and the first three of the second

explanation.surface: Someone is grounded after airport security at Heathrow.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is air travel, but the one who cannot fly is a bird; Heathrow is London's main airport.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the rhea is a large South American bird that cannot fly.

clue.text: Constituency with small majority / in the Borders? (8)

blocks.note: British political jargon for a seat that could change hands at the next election
the borders of a page are its margins; the question mark flags the pun

explanation.surface: A closely fought parliamentary seat in the Scottish Borders.
explanation.walkthrough: The Borders is a Scottish region, which makes this sound like election geography; with a small b, borders are the margins of a page.
explanation.definitionFit: British politics calls a narrowly held seat a marginal, and anything in the margins of a page is marginal too.

clue.text: Bully about to run after man (6)

indicators.note: the man comes first and the rest follows him

explanation.surface: A bully is about to chase after a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as a single idea meaning going to, but it splits into C and TO.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are verbs; the word comes from Hector of Troy, whose name came to mean a swaggering browbeater.

clue.text: Fighting almost tore apart densely populated area (6)

indicators.note: not quite all the word: drop its last letter

blocks.note: REND (tore apart) without its last letter

explanation.surface: Conflict nearly destroyed a crowded district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tore apart' looks like past-tense destruction; REND is the word it stands for.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative use from the rabbit's burrow system: a crowded maze of streets or rooms.

clue.text: Beginnings of days always witnessed now? (4)

definitions.text: Beginnings of days always witnessed now?

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, taken from each word that follows

blocks.note: one first letter from each of the four words

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the start of each day is always seen at the present moment.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: every day begins with first light, witnessed now.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes daybreak: the beginning of every day, seen as it arrives.

clue.text: Play-acting up to age nine starts to create empathy (8)

indicators.note: take the first letter of each following word

blocks.note: pre-ten: a child of nine or under

explanation.surface: Young children use make-believe to learn empathy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up to age nine' is a playful way of saying pre-ten, a child not yet ten.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean putting on a false show, as an actor does.

clue.text: Remove broadcast about all time to come (8)

indicators.note: seeds broadcast are scattered in all directions

blocks.note: re = about, as in memo headers; joins the fodder

explanation.surface: An instruction to take something off the air for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' looks like radio or TV, but it scatters REMOVE plus RE.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic word, as in 'for evermore': ever onwards, through all the time still to come.

clue.text: Type of punishment for petty officer (8)

definitions.note: 'Type of punishment' describes the adjective in corporal punishment

blocks.note: the kind inflicted on the body, from Latin corpus
petty = minor; wanted here is a junior army NCO rank

explanation.surface: Asking what penalty a junior naval officer should receive.
explanation.walkthrough: Petty officer is a naval rank, but here it just means a minor officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Corporal describes punishment of the body, and as a noun is a low army rank.

clue.text: Wrong-headed way to read poetry? (8)

blocks.note: per = by way of, one verse at a time

explanation.surface: A contrary suggestion for how poems should be read.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading poetry per verse, one verse at a time, is sensible; the joke is that the phrase spells the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone wrong-headed insists on the contrary view, which is being perverse.

clue.text: Truth is really breached by information technology (6)

indicators.note: a wall breached by something has it breaking in

blocks.note: IT = information technology, placed inside VER|Y

explanation.surface: The truth is badly compromised by computer systems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Really' reads as an intensifier but supplies VERY.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal synonym from Latin veritas, truth.

clue.text: Spot check (4)

blocks.note: a spot or blemish on a surface
what a teacher does to homework

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot check' reads as one phrase, a random inspection; split it into two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A mark is a spot on a surface, and marking work is checking it.

clue.text: Tune millions yodel badly (6)

indicators.note: done badly, the letters come out in the wrong order

explanation.surface: Millions of people yodel a tune out of key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' reads as a comment on the singing and is the anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the air of a song, the part you hum.

clue.text: 60 per cent of algorithms altered text praising God (6)

indicators.note: ALGORITHMS has ten letters, so keep the first six
the kept letters are changed around

blocks.note: first six of the ten letters of ALGORITHMS

explanation.surface: Computer code has tampered with a hymn.
explanation.walkthrough: The fraction is exact: six of ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gloria in excelsis Deo, 'glory to God in the highest', is the hymn of praise sung in the Mass.

clue.text: Flower I planted in lines close to rockery (4)

indicators.note: put inside, as a bulb in soil
the close of a word is its end, so take its last letter

explanation.surface: A gardener sets a flower in rows near the rock garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Planted' fits the gardening picture and is the container instruction; LL stands for lines, as in 'pp' for pages.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the lily is a garden flower grown from a bulb.

clue.text: Land mass is receding within America’s borders (4)

indicators.note: something receding moves back, so the word runs backwards
one word sits within another, inside its letters
the outer letters of the word

blocks.note: first and last letters of AmericA

explanation.surface: Land is being lost inside the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Receding' suggests coastal erosion, but it turns IS round.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a continent is a land mass, and Asia is the largest.

clue.text: Military Intelligence officer in contact with poet (6)

blocks.note: MI = Military Intelligence, as in MI5

explanation.surface: An intelligence officer is in touch with a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The spy story is all abbreviations; 'in contact with' means ON, as a hand on a table.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: John Milton wrote Paradise Lost.

clue.text: I chortle about tailor (8)

indicators.note: the letters are turned about

explanation.surface: Someone laughs about a tailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' reads as concerning, but it asks for the letters to be moved about.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: both make or sell garments, the clothier more broadly.

clue.text: Head of faculty’s area included in study (4)

indicators.note: one thing included in another sits among its parts, here among its letters

blocks.note: a den = a study, a private room

explanation.surface: A faculty head's floor space is part of a research study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Study' reads as research, but it is a room: a den.
explanation.definitionFit: The university title for the academic in charge of a faculty.
